🌱 Driving the Future of India’s Bioeconomy through Innovation!

Union Minister of Commerce and Industry, Shri Piyush Goyal, chaired a high-level roundtable on “India’s Bioeconomy Opportunity: Role of Startups in Driving Innovation and Growth”, organised by NITI Aayog Frontier Technology Hub in collaboration with Ministry of Commerce and Industry at Vanijya Bhawan, New Delhi.

The roundtable brought together policymakers, industry leaders and biopharma startups to deliberate on key enablers for strengthening India's bioeconomy.

Discussions focused on strengthening the biopharma startup ecosystem through faster regulatory approvals, a proposed Regulatory Sandbox, simplified patent processes, shared infrastructure, improved access to finance and Government schemes, indigenous manufacturing, and stronger inter-ministerial and industry–academia collaboration.

Shri Piyush Goyal emphasised leveraging India's scientific capabilities and entrepreneurial talent to position India as a global leader in the bioeconomy, with time-bound action on key recommendations.

The roundtable also featured insights from Ms. Debjani Ghosh, Distinguished Fellow, NITI Aayog, and Prof. Gobardhan Das, Member, NITI Aayog, highlighting the importance of research, collaboration and translating scientific innovations into commercially viable solutions.

A stronger startup ecosystem, enabling policies and collaborative action will be instrumental in unlocking India's immense bioeconomy potential.

#StartupSpotlight | ManasAI Technology Private Limited | IIT Mandi Catalyst

ManasAI Technology Private Limited, founded by Dr. Jyotiranjan Beuria (Founder), AKASH SHARMA (Co-Founder), and Inderjeet Nagpal (Co-Founder), is an IIT Mandi Catalyst-incubated startup. It is a research-driven company developing systems to sense and model inner well-being and understand the dynamics of the mind, without reducing individuals to mere dashboards or scores.

At the heart of its technology is a simple yet powerful idea: preserving access to raw data streams. This enables researchers to develop personalised, configurable AI models tailored to the needs of their specific studies or institutions, rather than relying on closed, one-size-fits-all scoring systems.

ManasAI aims to empower researchers with better instruments and greater flexibility to develop models that address individual needs.

What drives ManasAI?

🔹 Affordable, AI-powered devices that provide researchers with access to raw physiological signals, not just summary scores.
🔹 Physics-grounded models designed to reflect real-world dynamics, going beyond performance on benchmarks and leaderboards.
🔹 Consciousness as a scientific pursuit, approached through research rather than rhetoric.
🔹 A research-first philosophy: The device measures; it does not lecture.

Introducing SakshiSense
SakshiSense is the first offering in this technology stack a research-grade ring and wristband programme currently at the prototype and development stage.

Designed initially for research laboratories and centres, it aims to capture physiological signals such as PPG (photoplethysmography), motion, and skin conductance, while keeping the underlying data accessible for further research and analysis.

Through its innovations, ManasAI seeks to give researchers better tools, greater flexibility, and more opportunities to advance personalised research and the broader science of well-being.

For millions of smallholder farmers, climate change is not an abstract environmental challenge to debate at yet another conference or articulate in yet another report. It is an everyday economic reality. 

Unpredictable rainfall, water scarcity, declining soil health, rising input costs and uncertain crop yields directly affect household incomes and livelihood security. Women face additional disadvantages when technologies, productive assets and market opportunities are not designed around their needs.

These challenges are deeply interconnected. And so must be the solutions. 

This Lab to Land documentary series features six innovators working across soil health, water conservation, biological inputs, clean energy, agricultural mechanisation and sustainable farming. Each innovation approaches a different problem. But together, they illustrate something much larger.

𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗱𝗮𝗽𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗱𝘀. 𝗦𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝘃𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆. 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘄𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻 𝗴𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗲𝘀, 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘀, 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀.

And resilience is not simply the ability to survive the next shock. It is the capacity to become progressively less vulnerable while building greater economic opportunity. 

Entrepreneurship is about doing — taking risks, building solutions and demonstrating value. It can play a transformative role in building economic resilience, helping people improve their incomes, reduce costs, manage risks, adapt to climate change and build more secure livelihoods. But a technology must work reliably, demonstrate economic value, become affordable and accessible, and earn the trust of its users. For resource-constrained communities, experimenting with unproven technologies can be prohibitively risky. Someone must absorb those risks, validate solutions and help build the markets that make widespread adoption possible.

Our role is not simply to finance innovation. It is to help create the conditions in which innovation can succeed, markets can emerge, and impact can endure.

These six stories illustrate a larger proposition: economic prosperity, climate resilience, environmental sustainability and social inclusion need not be competing objectives. With the right innovations and institutions, they can reinforce one another.

Three weeks ago, we released 𝗟𝗮𝗯 𝘁𝗼 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗱, 𝗮𝗻 𝘂𝗻𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘆 (https://lnkd.in/p/gTn-8S3J). Then six short films, one for each innovator. All seven now sit in a single playlist: Lab to Land: Food Systems. (Link in the comments)

Watched back to back, one pattern is hard to miss. The science and engineering were hard. What came after was harder: 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁, 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻, 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱.

The stakes are not abstract. A smallholder who tries something new takes a real risk with the only income she has. Climate change raises that risk every season: erratic rain, rising heat, tired soil. Each of these innovations helps her adapt. Hold water longer. Spend less on inputs. Grow through the dry months. Cook without smoke. On a small farm, resilience is built one season at a time.

𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲, 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗲.

None of this is solved in a lab, and none of it fits neatly in a pitch deck. That is why lab to land is not a relay. It is a continuum, and someone has to own it end to end.

The second pattern is who stands at the end of that continuum. Most often, a woman.

The Soil Didis buy their own testing kits and run their own businesses. Women no longer carry spray pumps on their backs when the machine is built for their bodies. Kitchens that ran on smoke now run on a clean flame. And on the smallholder farm, it is often she who decides whether a new idea gets a place in the field.

This is not an accident. In agriculture, we have always started with the woman smallholder. Not as a beneficiary at the end of the chain, but as the user, the customer and increasingly the entrepreneur. Design for her, and the innovation works for everyone.

Thank you, Radhika Chandrasekhar , for seeing the story before we did, and to the six founding teams for letting the camera in, unpolished.

A moment of national recognition for iCreate portfolio startups at the Bharat RE Summit & Expo 2026 in New Delhi.

Two iCreate portfolio startups, Apeiro Energy and Tectonic Power Pvt. Ltd., had the opportunity to interact with the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Shri Narendra Modi, and showcase their indigenous innovations contributing to India's renewable energy and clean technology landscape.

Kalpit Prajapati, Founder of Apeiro Energy, highlighted the startup's low-wind-speed vertical turbine technology, designed to explore new possibilities for harnessing wind energy along railway tracks and highways.

Dr. Khushbu Patel (Butani), Co-Founder & CTO of Tectonic Power, showcased the company's indigenously developed, patented PBI-based composite membrane technology, which combines agricultural waste-derived nano-silica with Polybenzimidazole (PBI) for applications in green hydrogen electrolysers and high-temperature PEM fuel cells.

These interactions reflect the growing capabilities of India's deep tech startup ecosystem and the role of homegrown innovations in advancing the country's clean energy ambitions.

At iCreate, we remain committed to nurturing innovators and supporting startups developing technologies for a more sustainable future.
